plan: [Use the symmetric Bayes–Nash linear equilibrium for a 3rd-price auction with 5 bidders. For uniform values, the slope solves c = 4/(5 E[second-highest of 4]) and E = 3/5, giving c = 4/3. So bid b = (4/3)*v. With v = 26, b = 34.666..., round to $0.1 precision. This maximizes expected profit under the IID-uniform model.]

[Assume other bidders bid their true values. If I bid b and win, that means all four others ≤ b; then expected third-highest equals the second-highest among four draws = (3/5)b. Win probability = (b/49)^4. Expected profit = (b/49)^4*(18 - 0.6b). Maximize w.r.t b → b = (4/3)*18 = 24. So overbidding to $24 maximizes expected payoff under this model.]

[Third-price sealed-bid with 5 bidders: if opponents bid their values, my win probability when I bid b is (b/49)^4. Conditional on winning, the payment equals the second-highest of four opponents, with expected value 3/5·b. Expected profit = (b/49)^4·(21 − 0.6b). Maximizing this gives b = 28. I will bid $28.]

[The winner pays the third-highest bid. For 4 opponents the expected third-highest = (3/5)*49 = 29.4, well above my value 9. The chance the payment ≤9 is only ≈2.1%, so attempting to win has negative expected payoff. To maximize long-run profit, avoid winning this round by bidding the minimum (0), preventing losses from paying more than my private value.]

[I model a symmetric equilibrium for the 3rd-price auction with 5 bidders. Assuming linear strategies b=a*v, the best-response FOC yields a=4/3. Hence bid = (4/3)*value. With my value $20, this gives 26.666..., rounded to the $0.1 increment: $26.7. This strategy maximizes expected payoff against opponents using the same strategy under independent uniform values.]
